title: Consent through a professional interpreter: laparoscopic cholecystectomy

header.contentArea: Consent; communication across a language barrier
guidelineVersions: GMC Decision making and consent (in effect 9 November 2020; updated 13 December 2024 and 3 August 2026)
NHS England Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services in primary care (September 2018)
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11

related.why: The content of consent for laparoscopic cholecystectomy

brief.scenario: Mr Andrei Popescu, 45, a warehouse supervisor, has had three episodes of biliary colic. Ultrasound shows gallstones with a normal bile duct. He has been listed for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He speaks Romanian and very little English. His daughter, 19, has come with him.
brief.task: Discuss with the examiner how you would take consent from Mr Popescu.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Consent is only valid if he understands. A professional interpreter is how you make sure he does.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Accepting his daughter as interpreter because she is there and it's quicker.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd arrange a professional Romanian interpreter before starting the consent discussion."

grid.label: Arranging a professional interpreter
grid.fail: Proceeds in English, or uses the daughter by default.
grid.pass: Books a professional Romanian interpreter (face to face, video or telephone) for the consent discussion.
grid.high: Prefers face to face or video for consent; checks dialect and interpreter gender preference; briefs the interpreter first.

grid.label: Conducting the interpreted consultation
grid.fail: Talks to the interpreter in the third person ('tell him...') in long, technical sentences.
grid.pass: Faces and speaks to the patient, short chunks, plain words, pauses for interpretation, allows extra time.
grid.high: Asks the interpreter to interpret everything said, including side comments, and not to add advice; watches his non-verbal cues.

grid.label: Content of consent
grid.fail: Mentions only 'bleeding and infection', or omits alternatives.
grid.pass: Procedure, benefits, material risks (bile leak, bile duct injury, bleeding, infection, conversion to open), and alternatives including no operation.
grid.high: Asks what matters to him (his job, time off, lifting) and tailors risks to it; offers written information in Romanian.

grid.label: Checking understanding
grid.pass: Asks him to explain back, in his own words, what the operation is and its main risks.
grid.high: Recognises a language barrier is not lack of capacity: all practicable steps, including an interpreter, must be taken first.

grid.label: Daughter offers to interpret
grid.pass: Explains the risks: inaccurate or edited interpretation, confidentiality, pressure on him, burden on her; still offers a professional.
grid.high: If he insists, confirms his informed choice through the professional interpreter, away from her, and records it.

grid.label: Documentation
grid.pass: Records the interpreter's name or ID, language, mode, and that understanding was checked.
grid.high: Records his preferences and reasons; plans the same interpreter to confirm consent on the day of surgery.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: His daughter speaks good English, so I'd ask her to translate. It's quicker than booking someone.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you talk to him?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd tell her: 'Tell your dad it's a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anaesthetic.'

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How do you know he understands?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd ask if he understands, and if he nods, he signs.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What do you write in the notes?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd book a professional Romanian interpreter, face to face, video or telephone.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you run the consultation?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd face Mr Popescu and speak to him, not the interpreter, in short, plain sentences, pausing for interpretation, and allow extra time.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What the operation involves and why; the risks, including bile leak, bile duct injury, bleeding, infection and conversion to an open operation; and alternatives, including not operating.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How do you check he understands?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd ask him to tell me, in his own words, what the operation is and the main risks.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: His daughter offers to interpret. Fine?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd thank her but explain the risks: things can be missed or softened, he may not want to share everything with her, and it's a burden on her. I'd still use the professional interpreter.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The interpreter's name or ID, the language, how they joined, and that understanding was checked.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A professional Romanian interpreter, ideally face to face or video for consent. I'd check his dialect and whether he'd prefer a male or female interpreter, and brief the interpreter first.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd speak directly to him, in short chunks, and ask the interpreter to interpret everything, including anything said between them, without adding advice. I'd watch his face as well as listen.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The standard risks, but first I'd ask what matters to him. As a warehouse supervisor, lifting and time off work matter, so I'd tailor what I say to that. I'd give him written information in Romanian if we have it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He nods at everything. Does he have capacity?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Nodding isn't understanding. I'd use teach-back. A language barrier doesn't mean he lacks capacity: I must take all practicable steps to help him decide, and the interpreter is one of them.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd ask him through the professional interpreter, without her there, whether that's truly his choice. If it is, I'd respect it and record it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd record his preferences and book the same interpreter to confirm consent on the day of surgery.

failures.move: Using the daughter because she is there.
failures.consequence: Risks are softened or missed, he may withhold information in front of her, and consent may not be valid.
He signs without understanding the risk of bile duct injury; consent is not informed.

failures.move: Speaking to the interpreter about him in the third person.
failures.consequence: He is excluded from his own consultation and trust is lost.
Material risks such as bile duct injury and conversion are not disclosed.

recovery.line: On reflection, for consent I'd use a professional interpreter and ask him privately what he prefers.
Not understanding English isn't a lack of capacity; I need to help him understand first.

knowledge.fact: Use an interpreter or translation service if a patient has difficulty understanding spoken English; check they have understood.

Always offer a registered interpreter; relying on family or friends is strongly discouraged. If the patient wants a relative, get his informed consent in his own language, independently of them, and record it.
Nobody under 16 should interpret, except when immediate and necessary treatment is needed.
A person is not unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help them have failed.
Disclose material risks: those a reasonable person in his position would consider significant, or that he would.

recall.think: Invalid consent: he signs without understanding the risks.
recall.say: "I'd book a professional Romanian interpreter for the consent discussion."
do: Professional interpreter; speak to him directly
Record interpreter details and his preferences

numbers.meaning: never interpreters, except immediate necessary treatment
all practicable steps before judging capacity

recall.trap: A relative who speaks good English.
recall.finish: Informed consent through a professional interpreter, confirmed again on the day.

sources.name: GMC: Decision making and consent

sources.supports: Use an interpreter or translation service; share information in a format the patient prefers (para 27); check understanding (para 30); record decisions and who made them (para 51); a consent form is no substitute for dialogue (para 55)

sources.name: NHS England: Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services in primary care
sources.supports: Always offer a registered interpreter; reliance on family or friends strongly discouraged (principle 6); if a patient wants a relative, informed consent sought independently in their own language and recorded (principle 7); under 16s not to interpret except immediate and necessary treatment (principle 8). Written for primary care; the principles are widely applied

partner.opening: Mr Popescu is in clinic with his daughter. Tell me how you would take consent for his operation.
partner.actorBrief: You are the examiner and lead a structured discussion. Ask the push questions in order. After the candidate describes the consultation, say: "His daughter says her English is good and offers to interpret." If the candidate accepts, move on without comment. Use the curveballs if time allows.

reveals.finding: He supervises a warehouse and worries about time off and lifting.
He explains the operation but says the risks are 'only pain'.

push.question: How would you arrange the consultation?
push.expect: Professional Romanian interpreter, face to face or video preferred for consent.

push.question: How would you speak to him?
push.expect: Directly, short chunks, plain words, pauses, extra time.

push.question: What would you tell him?
push.expect: Procedure, benefits, material risks including bile duct injury and conversion, alternatives.

push.question: His daughter offers to interpret. What do you do?
push.expect: Explains risks; still uses the professional interpreter; if he insists, confirms his choice privately and records it.

push.question: What do you document?
push.expect: Interpreter's name or ID, language, mode, understanding checked, his preferences.

curveballs.prompt: Only his 15-year-old son is with him today.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not acceptable for consent: under 16s interpret only when immediate treatment is needed. Use a professional interpreter.

curveballs.prompt: No face-to-face interpreter is free today.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Use a telephone or video interpreter; the operation is elective, so if that fails, rebook rather than proceed.
Ask him privately if he is comfortable; offer a different interpreter for confidentiality.

curveballs.prompt: He nods throughout. Does he lack capacity?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: a language barrier isn't incapacity. Teach-back through the interpreter first.
